/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import math
for k in [2,3,4]:
 n=2**(2**k)
 eps=1e-8
 w=(1-eps)/n
 wp=(1+eps)/n
 t=math.floor(math.log2(math.log2(1/w)))
 tp=math.floor(math.log2(math.log2(1/wp)))
 rotations=sum(1/j for j in range(1,n+1))-1
 print({'n':n, 'old_tier':t,'new_tier':tp,'log2_weight_ratio':math.log2(wp/w),'expected_rotations_at_endpoint':rotations})
n=1000
harmonic=sum(1/j for j in range(1,n+1))
random_mean_depth=2*(n+1)/n*harmonic-3
print({'uniform_n':n,'learned_tier':math.floor(math.log2(math.log2(n))), 'mean_depth_both_treaps':random_mean_depth,'expected_total_node_visits_20000_searches':20000*random_mean_depth})
for k in [3,4,5]:
 log2B=2**k
 probs=[2.0**(-(2**j)) for j in range(k+1)]
 tiers=[math.floor(math.log2((2**j)/log2B)) for j in range(k+1)]
 print({'log2_B':log2B,'weights_sum':sum(probs),'distinct_tiers':tiers,'tier_separated_depth':len(tiers),'log_B_inverse_last_weight':1})
PY"

strengths: The composite priority construction is simple and interpretable. The tier-size and harmonic ancestor arguments support an O(1 + log(1/w_x)) expected-depth bound for BSTs, removing the distribution and key-order restrictions of the frequency-only baseline.

The static analysis provides a meaningful cross-entropy upper bound, equivalently O(m[1 + H(p) + D_KL(p||q)]). The adversarial examples also help explain why deterministic frequency priorities and single-logarithm tiers can perform poorly.
The observation that reciprocal-square working-set weights have bounded total mass and change only when the corresponding item is accessed is useful for designing dynamic search structures.
weaknesses: The claimed weight-update bound is false for the proposed discretized priorities. In Corollary 2.7, take n = 2^(2^k), give all keys weights just below 1/n, and increase an endpoint key's weight to just above 1/n. Its tier improves, making it the root and requiring Theta(log n) expected rotations, although |log(w'/w)| can be arbitrarily small. Appendix C's delete-and-reinsert argument also establishes a sum of access costs, not their logarithmic difference. This undermines the update guarantees and the dynamic proofs that invoke them.

The B-tree depth proof in Theorem C.2 ignores negative tiers, which occur whenever w_x > 1/B. The construction explicitly puts different tiers in separate blocks. For B = 2^(2^k), ordered keys with weights 2^(-2^j), j = 0,...,k, form k+1 successive tier blocks, although the last key has log_B(1/w_x) = 1. Padding with sufficiently small weights satisfies the stated n and B conditions. Thus the claimed constant depth fails for the specified construction. The high-probability argument also assumes a per-tier size condition that is not established.

Several robustness conclusions exceed what their proofs establish. Theorem D.2, and consequently Theorem 4.5, substitutes actual cost(X,w) for an upper bound on that cost; this does not prove an additive comparison between actual costs. Likewise, Theorem 2.13 supplies a cross-entropy upper bound, not the 'exact' KL overhead described in the overview. Corollary C.6 additionally assumes control of tiny predicted probabilities that does not follow from an L-infinity error bound. Its dependent distance guarantees require regularization or a different argument.

The experiments fail a basic consistency check. Under exact uniform predictions, every key has the same tier, so learn-bst and random-treap have identical tree distributions. Figure 4 nevertheless shows a substantial, consistent advantage for learn-bst. With n = 1000, both should have approximately 12 expected visited nodes per uniform search, which also conflicts with the reported totals for m = 20000 if all accesses are counted. The text alternates between varying unique items and varying accesses. Shared counting rules, precise workload definitions, and reproducible implementations are needed before the empirical advantage is convincing. Dynamic updates and the B-tree extension are not experimentally evaluated.

The originality of the static guarantee is insufficiently established relative to classical weighted randomized search trees. Weighted treaps using exponential priorities with rates proportional to weights already achieve O(1 + log(W/w_x)) expected depth. The manuscript should explain what the composite priorities add beyond this approach and compare against it. Useful combinations can constitute contributions, but the unsupported extension guarantees currently carry much of the claimed additional significance.

Smaller corrections include the missing additive constant in depth bounds and the corresponding m term in entropy-based total costs, undefined previous-access values before a key's first access, and inconsistent high-probability notation. These are repairable presentation issues, distinct from the substantive counterexamples and experimental inconsistencies above.
